# How to make your models fast {.unnumbered}

Inference optimization has a funny way of looking like black magic from the outside. Someone changes a memory layout, adds a strange-looking kernel, or flips a serving flag—and suddenly the same model runs twice as fast.

But there is no magic here. There is computation, memory, communication, and a piece of hardware trying very hard to do exactly what we asked it to do. The difficult part is learning to see what we *actually* asked it to do.

That is what this book is about.

I am on a journey to understand how LLM inference becomes fast, starting from the lowest level I can reasonably reach: writing kernels, counting FLOPs, counting bytes, measuring what happens, and then figuring out why the numbers do not match the story in my head.

This is not meant to be a collection of optimization tricks. Tricks are difficult to remember and even harder to transfer to a new problem. I want to build a way of thinking that survives the next GPU, the next model architecture, and the next inference engine.

## The question we will keep asking

Every chapter comes back to one question:

> What is stopping this workload from going faster—compute, memory, communication, or the way we mapped the algorithm onto the hardware?

We will begin with a mathematical estimate. How much work is there? How much data must move? Given the machine underneath us, how long *should* this take?

Then we will write the obvious implementation and measure it.

Sometimes the estimate and the measurement will agree. More often, the GPU will politely inform us that our mental model is incomplete. That disagreement is where the useful learning begins.

## Why inference?

Training gets most of the dramatic GPU diagrams, but inference has its own set of wonderfully annoying problems. Prefill and decode behave differently. Batching improves throughput while fighting latency. The KV cache quietly eats memory. Quantization saves bandwidth but introduces new work. A kernel can be mathematically cheap and still spend most of its life waiting for data.

And I am betting heavily on small models. If small models are going to replace larger, more expensive systems in production, training them well is only half the job. We also need to make them cheap enough, fast enough, and predictable enough to serve everywhere they are useful.

## How to read this book

You do not need to know CUDA wizardry before starting. A basic understanding of machine learning and some comfort reading code should be enough. Whenever we introduce a hardware concept, we will introduce it because a real implementation has forced us to care about it.

The chapters are worklogs, not victory laps. I will keep the naive implementations, wrong assumptions, profiler surprises, and awkward intermediate versions. Seeing only the final kernel tells us what to type. Seeing why every earlier version failed teaches us how to find the next optimization ourselves.

For each problem, we will try to leave with four things:

- a mathematical model of the work;
- an implementation we can run;
- measurements we can challenge; and
- a mental model worth carrying into the next problem.

This book is a draft and will keep changing as I learn. If something is wrong, unclear, or suspiciously hand-wavy, [open an issue](https://github.com/athleticcoder21/inference-book/issues). That is part of the process too.

## The path through the book

The chapters are arranged from the inside of a GPU outward. That order is
intentional: serving-level optimizations become much easier to reason about
once we can recognize the bottleneck in the operation underneath them.

1. **Kernels.** Memory layout, tiling, reductions, and the GPU execution model.
   We start here with GEMV—the operation that makes decode so sensitive to
   memory bandwidth.
2. **Transformer inference.** How the shapes and costs of attention, MLPs,
   and the KV cache change between prefill and decode.
3. **Serving systems.** Batching, scheduling, cache management, quantization,
   and the latency/throughput/cost trade-offs of a real inference service.
4. **Scaling out.** Tensor, pipeline, and expert parallelism; communication;
   and choosing an architecture that keeps a fleet efficient.

New chapters will join this outline as runnable worklogs, with the code and
measurements kept in this repository.

## Start here

The first chapter takes the most innocent-looking operation possible—a matrix multiplied by a vector—and follows it all the way down to the memory transactions generated by a warp.
